Longitudinal Mixed-Model Calibration Simulation (Goal 5a)

mlmRev::egsingle two-stage hierarchical plasmode resampling

2026-11-05

1 Purpose

This report documents Goal 5a of the RESI mixed-model extension project (see instructions/instructions.md and log/claudeLog.md at the repository root): a calibration check of the simulation machinery for lme4::lmer before any RESI confidence-interval theory is layered on top. It collects, in one place: the dataset used, the simulation settings, the diagnostics that identified a fixed-effect SE mis-calibration under full bootstrap resampling of the real data, and the hybrid plasmode simulation, which is now the primary validation method for calibration going forward (see the note below).

2 Note: full bootstrap (plasmode) resampling does not produce consistent SEs

Earlier work in this project ran longitudinalCalibrationSim(), which resamples the real egsingle data with a two-stage with-replacement cluster bootstrap (draw schools with replacement, then draw children with replacement within each drawn school) and refits Model A/B on each resampled dataset. That full-bootstrap approach produced fixed-effect model-based standard errors that were not consistent with the true (Monte Carlo) sampling variability of the estimates: mean_model_se / mc_sd plateaued well below 1 for child- and occasion-level covariates (female, black, hispanic, year), and the between-school variance component (var_schoolid) showed substantial, growing bias as the number of resampled schools grew. This pattern held on both the real data and a synthetic dataset generated from the same fitted model, and was not fully resolved by decoupling the number of sites from the number of subjects per site (see the diagnostic sections below for that history).

Simon’s hypothesis: this failure is caused by real slope variation across the sampling levels (e.g. schools and children have their own, slightly different coefficients for covariates such as year, female, black, hispanic) that is not included in the model formula (Model A only has random intercepts, not random slopes, for these covariates). When the real data is resampled with replacement, this unmodeled cross-level slope heterogeneity is present in every replicate and inflates the true sampling variability of the fixed-effect estimates beyond what the fitted model’s SE formula – which assumes the random-intercept-only structure is correct – can capture. This is consistent with the slope-heterogeneity diagnostic below, which found that removing true slope heterogeneity from the data-generating process (a synthetic outcome simulated directly from Model A’s own fitted parameters, with no unmodeled heterogeneity by construction) recovers correct SE calibration.

The hybrid plasmode simulation (see the dedicated section below) is the primary method used to validate calibration. It resamples schools and students hierarchically, preserving the empirical covariate distribution, then generates new outcomes from the fitted Model A using rescaled empirical BLUP pools and fresh residuals. Thus covariates are resampled, but real outcomes are not; the generated outcome follows the specified random- intercept model. Replicate fits now use REML. The earlier full-bootstrap results and code remain available in tests/ and RESI/R/simulations.R for reference.

3 Dataset: mlmRev::egsingle

egsingle is a 3-level growth-curve dataset (measurement occasion nested in child nested in school) used as the plasmode base because it is the only dataset found (across lme4, nlme, geepack, mlmRev, JM, joineR, merTools) with >=1000 independent subjects, a continuous repeated-measures outcome, and a continuous time covariate suitable for a smooth term.

Every one of the 60 schools has at least 5 children, up to 89, with a mean of 28.7 and median of 24 children per school (SD 18.1) – a right-skewed, moderately variable cluster-size distribution, which is why the plasmode resampling below draws each school’s own number of children (not a fixed number) when it is resampled.

3.3 Variables

egsingle variables and nesting structure
Variable Level Type Description
schoolid 3 (school, n=60) factor school identifier
childid 2 (child, n=1721) factor child identifier, nested in school
year 1 (occasion, n=7230 rows) continuous time, centered (range -2.5 to 2.5, integer steps)
grade 1 (occasion) continuous (0-4) grade level, collinear with year

retained 1 (occasion) binary factor held back a grade (mostly time-invariant)

black 2 (child) binary factor child race indicator
hispanic 2 (child) binary factor child ethnicity indicator
size 3 (school) continuous school enrollment size
lowinc 3 (school) continuous % low income at school
mobility 3 (school) continuous % student mobility at school

4 Simulation design

4.1 Fixed-divisor covariate rescaling

size (school enrollment, range 113-1486, SD 312.6) is on a very different scale from the other covariates and caused an lme4 convergence warning when used raw. Both size and lowinc are rescaled by a fixed divisor (not a z-score), applied identically to every replicate, so coefficients stay directly interpretable:

  • size_100 = size / 100 (school enrollment in hundreds of students)
  • lowinc_10 = lowinc / 10 (percent low-income in units of 10 percentage points)

Combined with lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5)), both models below fit with 0 convergence warnings on the full data.

4.2 Models A and B

Shared fixed effects: math ~ year + female + black + hispanic + size_100 + lowinc_10

  • Model A (random intercepts only): `+ (1 | schoolid/childid)`
  • Model B (random slope for year at the child level): `+ (1 + year | childid) + (1 | schoolid)`

The full-sample Model A fit uses ML (REML = FALSE) and supplies the plug-in generating parameters and full-sample reference. Each simulated Model A fit uses REML (REML = TRUE). Thus the replicate estimator is REML while the full-sample target/generating fit is ML; interpret finite-sample differences with that distinction in mind.

4.3 Full-outcome two-stage plasmode bootstrap (deprecated)

An earlier version of this simulation resampled the real data directly in two stages (schools with replacement, then children with replacement within each drawn school). As documented in the note above, this full-bootstrap approach does not produce fixed-effect SEs consistent with the true sampling variability, so it is no longer used for calibration; see RESI/R/simulations.R (.longSimResampleHierarchical()) for the implementation if needed for reference.

Random-effect (variance component) standard errors are not computed by any of the simulations below; only fixed-effect model-based SEs are compared against the Monte Carlo SD of each fixed effect across replicates. Variance-component point estimates are still tracked for bias.

5 Hybrid plasmode (hierarchical covariate and BLUP resampling)

5.1 Motivation and method

This hybrid plasmode resamples the covariate design hierarchically from the real data, then generates fresh random effects and residuals from the fitted Model A generator. This retains the empirical joint covariate distribution across schools and students without carrying over the real outcomes.

For each replicate, draw n_schools source schools with replacement from the 60 observed schools. Within each selected source school, draw students with replacement. If source school \(i\) contains \(m_i\) observed students, draw approximately \(n_{per\_site} m_i / \bar m\) students, where \(\bar m\) is the average observed school size. Thus expected sample size is proportional to source-school size and the average number drawn per generated school is approximately n_per_site; rounding makes the realized total vary slightly. Each selected student contributes all of their observed measurement rows. Every school and student draw receives a new ID, even when the same source school or student is selected more than once. This sampling is with replacement and occurs anew for every replicate.

Raw BLUPs are shrunk toward zero relative to the true random-effect variance (a well-known property of best linear unbiased prediction), so each BLUP pool is first centered to exactly mean zero and then rescaled so its variance equals the corresponding fitted variance component before any resampling: \[b^*_i = (b_i - \bar b) \times \sqrt{\hat\sigma^2 / \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(b - \bar b)}\] For Model A fit to the real data: the 60 school BLUPs have raw variance 0.056 (fitted var_schoolid = 0.079, so rescale factor \(\approx 1.19\)); the 1721 child BLUPs have raw variance 0.562 (fitted var_childid:schoolid = 0.652, rescale factor \(\approx 1.08\)). The full-data Model A fit remains ML (REML = FALSE) and supplies the plug-in DGP fixed effects and variance components. School and student BLUP pools are centered and rescaled to their fitted variances; each generated school and student receives an independent draw with replacement from its corresponding pool. Fresh residuals are drawn from the fitted Normal residual distribution. Each simulated dataset is refit using REML (REML = TRUE); the coefficient and RESI standard errors are model-based, from stats::vcov.

The reported grid is n_schools in {15,30,60,100} crossed with n_per_site in {25,100,200}. The 200-school and 50-student/site conditions are excluded. The simulation sets set.seed(2026) once before iterating over grid cells. mclapply uses L’Ecuyer-CMRG worker streams with mc.set.seed = TRUE for covariate resampling, BLUP resampling, and residual draws.

5.2 Results

Blank entries in the wide tables indicate conditions that were not simulated. The RESI table reports the mean and SD of the realized student count across replicates (n and n_sd), since proportional cluster-size sampling does not yield exactly n_schools * n_per_site students in every replicate. For the third plot row, the intercept and school-level predictors use n_schools; student-level and time-varying predictors use the planned student count n_schools * n_per_site. The realized student count and its SD are reported separately. This follows the between-school versus within-school scaling principle of Lyu and Welsh, treating repeated observations per student as bounded for this comparison. The full-sample ML SE, scaled by the square root of its full-sample reference count, is fixed across designs. Each cell’s Monte Carlo SD of coefficient error is scaled by the square root of its planned count (n_schools for school-level terms; n_schools * n_per_site for student/time terms), then divided by that fixed full-sample scaled SE. Dashed curves show these ratios; the solid horizontal reference is 1.

The third row shows scaled Monte Carlo coefficient-error SD divided by the fixed scaled full-sample ML SE; dashed term-colored curves are compared with the solid reference at 1. Intercept and school-level terms use n_schools; student/time terms use n_schools times n_per_site. Other rows show fixed-effect SE ratios, variance-component relative bias, RESI coefficient bias, and RESI ANOVA-term bias. Columns are n_schools values; y-scales are shared within each row.

5.3 RESI point-estimator calibration

For each coefficient and ANOVA term, the table compares the full-data RESI reference with the mean, bias, and empirical SD of replicate RESI estimates. The reference uses the full-sample ML fit; simulated datasets are refit by REML. Both use the same model-based covariance function (stats::vcov) and student-level normalizer (level = 2), with the fitted student count n recorded for each design. Variation level describes where the fixed-effect design term changes. These metrics calibrate the RESI point estimator only, not its sampling variance or confidence intervals; that covariance theory remains future work.

5.4 Interpretation

  • Fixed-effect SE calibration and variance-component bias are shown across the joint n_schools by n_per_site grid, with common y-axis limits across columns within each row.
  • The RESI rows show coefficient- and ANOVA-term point-estimator bias against the model-based full-data target. These are point-estimator diagnostics; covariance and confidence-interval calibration for RESI remains future work.

6 Open questions / next steps

  • Simon’s slope-heterogeneity hypothesis (see the note above) explains why full bootstrap resampling of the real data fails to produce consistent SEs, but has not been separately, directly confirmed for every affected term (it fully explains year’s mis-calibration in the earlier slope-heterogeneity diagnostic, but not the full extent of the child-level-covariate or var_schoolid patterns). In the current hybrid simulation, the covariate design is resampled but outcomes are generated from Model A, so no random slopes are introduced into the outcome model.
  • The reported RESI uses the student-level count as a common normalizer. The calibration tables report the mean and SD of the realized student count under proportional within-school sampling.
  • For 100 schools, source-school covariate profiles are sampled repeatedly from the observed 60-school empirical distribution. Assessing sensitivity to this finite school-profile pool remains an interpretation caveat.
